BEFORE THE ILLINOIS WORKERS’ COMPENSATION COMMISSION 
 
 
Barry Nichols, 
 
 
Petitioner, 
 
 
vs. 
No.  23 WC 28326 
 
 
TriStar, 
 
 
Respondent. 
 
DECISION AND OPINION ON REVIEW 
 
Timely Petition for Review under §19(b) having been filed by Petitioner herein and notice 
given to all parties, the Commission, after considering the issues of causal connection, medical 
expenses, prospective medical care, temporary disability, maintenance, permanent disability, 
penalties and attorney fees, and being advised of the facts and law, modifies the Decision of the 
Arbitrator as stated below and otherwise affirms and adopts the Decision of the Arbitrator, which 
is attached hereto and made a part hereof.  The Commission further remands this case to the 
Arbitrator for further proceedings for a determination of a further amount of temporary total 
compensation, medical benefits or of compensation for permanent disability, if any, pursuant to 
Thomas v. Industrial Comm’n, 78 Ill.2d 327 (1980). 
 
The Commission adopts the Arbitrator’s chronological statement of facts, but not the 
ultimate findings or conclusions.  With regard to the statement of facts, the Commission makes 
the following corrections:  
 
• Scrivener’s error p. 3, ¶ 3.  The Commission strikes “November 9, 2022” and 
replaces it with “February 1, 2024.” 
 
• Scrivener’s error p. 3, last paragraph.  The Commission strikes “2023” and replaces 
it with “2022.” 
 
Turning to substantive issues, the main issue is causation.  The Arbitrator found no 
causation on the basis of “the gap of treatment, no causation opinion [from a treating physician] 
26IWCC0136

23 WC 28326 
Page 2 
 
and Petitioner’s inconsistent testimony.”  The Arbitrator further found: “In contrast, Respondent 
provided the opinion of Dr. Neault who opined Petitioner sustained a temporary condition with 
the alleged work-related injury. He noted his right shoulder surgery addressed chronic, 
degenerative issues and not addressed any acute injury. He also noted his diabetes was likely why 
he developed adhesive capsulitis. (RX2, Ex.2). The Arbitrator notes there is no opinion to refute 
this explanation.”   
 
While Dr. Neault opined in his report that Petitioner’s condition reached MMI about one 
year after the initial injury, the Commission, however, highlights Dr. Neault’s testimony on cross-
examination. (RX2).  Dr. Neault opined that Petitioner “had a strain of his right shoulder, and then 
he developed adhesive capsulitis.”  The adhesive capsulitis appeared to be causally related to the 
accident.  The following colloquy then took place: 
 
“Q. Let’s assume that the shoulder pain set in with the fall on the shoulder, 
and persisted up until the time of the surgery, and hopefully resolved with the 
surgery ***. 
 
But let’s assume there’s contiguity between the accident and the time the 
surgery was done. At least some of those preexisting conditions must have been 
aggravated in this fall onto the shoulder directly during this accident, leading to at 
least part of the surgical techniques you [sic] performed in July of ’24, would you 
agree? 
 
A. I guess that there’s a chance that there could be some contribution from 
that. But again, it’s not really acute findings at that point.” 
 
Dr. Neault agreed that a partial tear or undersurface tear of the supraspinatus, as seen on the MRI 
and noted in the operative report, could also cause pain.  Upon further questioning, Dr. Neault 
added: “[H]is shoulder did, kind of, wax and wane a bit in the record with his range of motion and 
whatnot.”  The colloquy continued: 
 
“Q. So you would concede though, that the pain from the fall on the 
shoulder never went away before the surgery; correct? 
 
A. The pain changed in character before the surgery, but he did continue to 
have some form of pain up until the surgery. 
 
Q. *** And up until the therapy and the injection improved the range of 
motion—I mean, he had range of motion limitations from the date of accident 
forward; correct? 
 
A. Yes. 
 
Q. Okay. You understand that the very first note at the emergency room was 
a diagnosis of rotator cuff injury; correct? 
 
26IWCC0136

23 WC 28326 
Page 3 
 
A. Yes. 
 
Q. Okay. And then you saw the doctors at Castle initially identified it as 
right shoulder pain, which is a generalized diagnosis, and then a right rotator cuff 
tear; right? 
 
Yes.” 
 
Lastly, Dr. Neault admitted the operative diagnosis of subacromial impingement/aggravation of 
the bone spurs could be causally related to the accident.   
 
Based on the foregoing, the Commission finds that Dr. Neault provided a causation opinion 
in Petitioner’s favor.  Accordingly, the Commission reverses the Arbitrator on causation.  The 
Commission further notes that it is premature to make a determination of MMI.  Petitioner had an 
FCE on May 27, 2025, but had not followed up with his physician. 
 
Next, the Commission considers the issue of notice.  The Commission strikes the notice 
section.  We find Petitioner provided sufficient notice in his email to Linda Baker on November 
25, 2022.  The body of that email states: “I spoke with my doctor’s office and they indicated they 
sent twice. I have my next appointment scheduled for the 19th and will address this with him at 
that time. I was also referred to a orthopedic specialist for my right shoulder strain which occurred 
while lifting and moving my work computer for transfer to the Chicago office.” 
 
Having found in Petitioner’s favor on the issues of causation and notice, the Commission 
awards temporary total disability benefits from July 22, 2024 (the date of surgery) through 
November 22, 2024 (release to return to work with a 10-15 pound lifting restriction, no overhead 
work or forcible pushing/pulling).  These restrictions would have allowed Petitioner to perform 
his regular job.  Further, the Commission awards reasonable and related outstanding medical bills 
submitted in PX2 pursuant to Sections 8(a) and 8.2 of the Act. 
 
The Commission affirms the denial of penalties, but substitutes its own analysis.  The 
Commission notes that the record shows no demand for payment of medical bills and tender 
pursuant to Section 19(l).  Further, Petitioner failed to prove Respondent’s conduct was 
unreasonable or vexatious pursuant to Sections 19(k) and 16. 
 
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Decision of the 
Arbitrator filed September 26, 2025, is hereby modified as stated herein and otherwise affirmed 
and adopted. 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall pay to 
Petitioner the sum of $725.04 per week for a period of 17 5/7 weeks, from July 22, 2024 through 
November 22, 2024, that being the period of temporary total incapacity for work under §8(b), and 
that as provided in §19(b) of the Act, this award in no instance shall be a bar to a further hearing 
and determination of a further amount of temporary total compensation, medical benefits or of 
compensation for permanent disability, if any.  Respondent shall be given a credit of $14,025.40 
for temporary total disability benefits that have been paid. 
26IWCC0136

23 WC 28326 
Page 4 
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall pay 
reasonable and related outstanding medical bills submitted in PX2 pursuant to §§8(a) and 8.2 of 
the Act. 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that this case be remanded to the 
Arbitrator for further proceedings consistent with this Decision, but only after the latter of 
expiration of the time for filing a written request for Summons to the Circuit Court has expired 
without the filing of such a written request, or after the time of completion of any judicial 
proceedings, if such a written request has been filed. 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent pay to Petitioner 
interest under §19(n) of the Act, if any. 
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall have credit 
for all amounts paid, if any, to or on behalf of Petitioner on account of said accidental injury. 
 
Bond for the removal of this cause to the Circuit Court by Respondent is hereby fixed at 
the sum of $5,000.00.  The party commencing the proceedings for review in the Circuit Court shall 
file with the Commission a Notice of Intent to File for Review in Circuit Court.

An Application for Adjustment of Claim was filed in this matter, and a Notice of Hearing was mailed to each 
party.  The matter was heard by the Honorable Roma Dalal, Arbitrator of the Commission, in the city of 
Geneva, on June 30, 2025 and September 25, 2025 in Geneva.  After reviewing all of the evidence 
presented, the Arbitrator hereby makes findings on the disputed issues checked below, and attaches those 
findings to this document. 
 
DISPUTED ISSUES 
 
A. 
 Was Respondent operating under and subject to the Illinois Workers' Compensation or Occupational  
 
 Diseases Act? 
 
B. 
 Was there an employee-employer relationship? 
 
C. 
 Did an accident occur that arose out of and in the course of Petitioner's employment by Respondent? 
 
D. 
 What was the date of the accident? 
 
E.

J.

 paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and necessary medical services? 
 
K.

FINDINGS 
On the date of accident, November 9, 2022, Respondent was operating under and subject to the provisions of 
the Act.  
On this date, an employee-employer relationship did exist between Petitioner and Respondent.   
On this date, Petitioner did sustain an accident that arose out of and in the course of employment. 
Timely notice of this accident was given to Respondent. 
Petitioner's current condition of ill-being is not causally related to the accident.
In the year preceding the injury, Petitioner earned $56,553.12; the average weekly wage was $1,087.56. 
On the date of accident, Petitioner was 58 years of age, married with 0 dependent children. 
Respondent has paid all reasonable and necessary charges for all reasonable and necessary medical services.  
Respondent shall be given a credit of $14,025.40 for TTD, $0 for TPD, $0 for maintenance, and $0 for other 
benefits, for a total credit of $14,025.40. 
Respondent is entitled to a credit of $0 under Section 8(j) of the Act. 
ORDER 
The Arbitrator finds Petitioner’s current condition unrelated to his work injury. As such the Arbitrator 
declines to award benefits. 
In no instance shall this award be a bar to subsequent hearing and determination of an additional amount of 
medical benefits or compensation for a temporary or permanent disability, if any.   
RULES REGARDING APPEALS  Unless a party files a Petition for Review within 30 days after receipt of this 
decision, and perfects a review in accordance with the Act and Rules, then this decision shall be entered as the 
decision of the Commission.   
STATEMENT OF INTEREST RATE  If the Commission reviews this award, interest at the rate set forth on the Notice 
of Decision of Arbitrator shall accrue from the date listed below to the day before the date of payment; 
however, if an employee's appeal results in either no change or a decrease in this award, interest shall not 
accrue.

FINDINGS OF FACT 
This matter proceeded to hearing on June 30, 2025, in Geneva, Illinois before Arbitrator Dalal on 
Petitioner’s 19(b) Petition for Hearing. Issues in dispute include accident, causation, disputed medical 
bills, TTD benefits from November 9, 2022 through May 27, 2025, maintenance benefits from May 28, 
2025 through June 30, 2025, penalties and whether Petitioner is at maximum medical improvement. (T.5). 
The parties reopened proofs on September 25, 2025 to submit the Request for Hearing form into evidence. 
(Arb. Ex.1).  
Barry Nichols (hereinafter referred to as the “Petitioner”), testified he was employed by TriStar 
(hereinafter referred to as the “Respondent) on November 9, 2022. (T.8). Petitioner testified he was 
gathering his computer to go downtown Chicago. He noted the computer consisted of a tower metal stand, 
monitors, and two cameras, weighing approximately 50 pounds. (T.9). Petitioner testified that he had to 
take his whole computer set up to the office. (T.10). Initially Petitioner was employed as a worker’s 
compensation specialist. He would handle complex worker’s compensation cases from beginning to the 
end to include investigation, medical, and follow ups. (T.11). He was subsequently advanced to a pension 
specialist. (T.11). Petitioner alleged he had to come downtown more often with this job. (T.12).   
Petitioner alleges on November 9, 2022, he was required to pack his home computer up to travel 
into the city to work and in doing so, he did not realize the computer was still plugged into the wall and 
when he lifted it, it jerked, and he felt pain in his shoulder.  He testified he fell onto a couch landing on 
his right shoulder, and that he felt a popping sensation in his right shoulder and horrible pain. (T.12-13). 
Petitioner testified he felt pain the next day, so he went to the ER at Ascension Mercy. (T.16). He 
was recommended to follow up with his primary care physician. Petitioner testified he did not see any 
physician for 7 months. (T.17).  
26IWCC0136

2 
 
Petitioner testified he reported the injury after he started getting bills. (T.18). Petitioner testified on 
November 17, 2022 he emailed Linda Baker that he had a doctor’s appointment and was referred to an 
orthopedic specialist for his right shoulder strain which occurred while lifting and moving his work 
computer for transfer to the Chicago office. (T.20).    
Petitioner placed an email into evidence with the title “Barry Nichols FMLA Claim.” The email 
indicated he would address “this” with his physician on the 19th and noted he was also referred to an 
orthopedic specialist for his right shoulder strain which occurred while lifting and moving his work 
computer to the Chicago office. The email was dated November 25, 2022. (PX6).  
Petitioner testified that after he saw his primary care physician he proceeded to physical therapy at 
ATI. (T.22). He also saw an orthopedic specialist. (T.22). Petitioner testified his shoulder was very painful, 
and he could not lift or reach behind his back. (T.23).  
After physical therapy he was seen by Dr. Bansal at Castle Orthopaedics and was referred to Dr. 
Saleem. (T.24). He eventually underwent an injection into the shoulder and therapy. (T.24). Petitioner 
testified he underwent right shoulder surgery. (T.25). Petitioner testified when he would go to the doctor, 
he would ask them to be taken off of work. (T.26). Petitioner eventually underwent an FCE at ATI. (T.27). 
Petitioner testified from November 2022 through December 2023 he did not have any off-work 
notes. He indicated he was not able to do “stuff” because he was in pain. (T.28). Petitioner testified 
Respondent did not help him obtain treatment. (T.30). Petitioner has not worked anywhere since the 
accident. (T.31). As of February 5, 2024 Dr. Bansal placed Petitioner on restrictions of 5 pounds. (T.31). 
Petitioner further testified he has not reinjured his arm since the work accident. (T.32).  
Petitioner testified his daily activities are limited. It is hard to cut grass and drive. It is hard to lift 
his pet, wash dishes, or mop floors. (T.33). He further noted he cannot ride his bike or sleep well. (T.34). 
Petitioner noted his pet was a 10-pound chihuahua. (T.34).  
On Cross-Examination, Petitioner testified he was a claims adjuster with Respondent. His duties 
included taking and making phone calls. He would input claim information, issue weekly payments, and 
send emails. All those tasks were a sedentary position. (T.36-37).  
Petitioner acknowledged on November 29, 2021 he received a letter from Respondent indicating 
that his job was a remote position from home. (T.38).  Respondent placed a letter into evidence noting 
Petitioner was offered the position of Claims Examiner II, working remotely from home. (RX5).  
Petitioner acknowledged his direct supervisors were  Mackenzie Gill and Michelle Woodson (T.39). 
He did not report his injuries to them. (T.40). Instead, he advised Linda Baker, who was in the benefits 
department. (T.40). He was unsure whether she was affiliated with worker’s compensation.  
Petitioner noted that on September 21, 2022 he advised Mackenzie Gill he wouldn’t be in the office 
due to health issues and was taking a medical leave. (T.41). The medical leave was September 19, 2022 
through March 20, 2023 for personal reasons. (T.41-42). This was for an esophageal varices for cirrhosis. 
(T.42). Petitioner noted he was not sure if the leave of absence was denied. (T.43).  
26IWCC0136

3 
 
Petitioner testified that he changed jobs from a worker’s compensation adjuster to a pension 
adjuster in March or April of 2022. (T.44). He also noted that he received an email on September 7, 2022 
indicating there appeared to be an overpayment in a worker’s compensation award by $24,000.00. (T.45; 
RX6). The Arbitrator notes that this email suggests he was still working as a worker’s compensation 
adjuster as of September 2022.  
Petitioner confirmed he had treatment for his balance prior to this injury. (T.49). Petitioner indicated 
he was not sure if he used cannabis on the day of the accident. (T.55). He also confirmed that he was 
involved in a motor vehicle accident and noted he was not driving. (T.50).  
Petitioner testified that on November 9, 2022 he asked his doctor to provide him a causation opinion 
and that this was the first time he requested the same. He also confirmed that he was an experienced claims 
adjuster and familiar with the requirements for causation opinions and work status notes in order to be 
entitled to benefits. (T.52-53). He confirmed he did not ask for anything until about a year and a half after 
the accident. (T.53).  
Petitioner indicated he was truthful and honest with Dr. Neault, the Section 12 examiner, but did 
not tell him he was working until the surgery. (T.56)  
Petitioner noted he did not review his FCE and did not know he tested out at the medium capacity. 
(T.60). Petitioner indicated that a claims adjuster position is not always sedentary as he has to stand 
sometimes. (T.62). He confirmed he does not lift heavy items as a claims adjuster. (T.63). Petitioner 
testified that mainly his job was in the level of the FCE but not always. (T.65). He testified he has to lift 
reports and do reports. He would have to carry files and reports. (T.65-66). He further testified that he 
would put files in a filing cabinet. (T.66). Later he stated at the time of the accident he did not have an 
obligation to keep files and put them in a file cabinet. (T.66). He also indicated he told one of the doctors 
he did heavy reports. (T.67). He clarified that he was just typing them into the computer, and nothing was 
heavy about that. (T.67).  
Petitioner has not been back to the doctor and testified he was supposed to follow up after the FCE 
but has not scheduled an appointment and was waiting for the doctor’s office to schedule it. (T.67-68).   
Petitioner clarified that the motor vehicle accident was when he was sitting in his car at the service 
department and one of the porters backed into the back of the car in the rear. (T.69).  
Petitioner confirmed he did not advise his immediate managers of the work accident. (T.72).  
Petitioner placed an itemization of medical bills into evidence, several were unrelated to the alleged 
injury. (PX2). Petitioner also placed a picture of his work set up into evidence. (PX5).  
Medical Summary 
Petitioner was already treating with specialists at Rush Copley for significant medical issues 
unrelated to the work accident. (PX1). He had a visit for balance issues in late October of 2023. (PX1 
p.1266). Petitioner was in physical therapy due to dizziness, unsteadiness on his feet and abnormal gait.  
26IWCC0136

4 
 
He was undergoing treatment at Amita Health Mercy Medical Center. Id. at 1267. The physical therapy 
notes from October 31, 2022 documented that one of the goals was to improve Petitioner’s balance to 
improve his ability to perform yard work. Id. at 1275. The physical therapy notes on October 26, 2022 
also reflect that Petitioner was having difficulty with lifting heavy objects and that he was a claims adjuster 
who did a lot of sitting. Id. at 1277. 
Petitioner also had ongoing treatment for a GI bleed, cirrhosis, and esophageal varices. (PX1). He 
actively treated for these conditions after the accident, including admission to Mercy for a GI bleed on 
January 4, 2023, undergoing testing and workup. (PX1 p.1197). Surgery was performed on January 6, 
2023 for a significant issue unrelated to the accident. Id. at 1198. The gastroenterologist reported at the 
May 23, 2023 visit that Petitioner’s unrelated issues were doing better. Id. at 1220.  
 On November 10, 2022, Petitioner presented to Amita Health in Aurora. The hospital intake 
documented Petitioner was unemployed and his primary insurance was listed as Meridian Health. (PX4 
p. 17).  Petitioner was a 58-year-old male presenting after a fall yesterday. He reported pain in his right 
shoulder and left lower quadrant. The doctor suspected contusion versus rotator cuff injury. Petitioner was 
given medication and was to follow up with orthopedics. Id. at 45-46.  
On December 19, 2022, Petitioner was seen by his primary care physician, Dr. Aiyash for a follow 
up on his Type 2 diabetes mellitus. There was no mention of any shoulder issues.  The note from this date 
did, however, indicate that Petitioner was unemployed, despite Petitioner’s testimony that he did not know 
he had been terminated from his job with Respondent and thought he was still employed as of the date of 
trial. (PX1, p.1244-1247).  
Petitioner returned to Dr. Aiyash on January 19, 2023. This visit was for a follow-up after his 
January 4, 2023 emergency room visit after finding blood in his urine. (PX1, p.1227-1231). 
Petitioner returned to Dr. Aiyash on March 23, 2023 for his type 2 diabetes and hypertension. There 
is no documentation of any shoulder pain. (PX1, p.1200).  
On June 8, 2023,  Kristin Engle, PA ordered right shoulder X-rays. (PX1, p.1180). Right shoulder 
X-rays were done on June 8, 2023. Id. at 1181. There is no indication why this was ordered.  
Petitioner then presented to Castle Orthopedics on July 13, 2023.  He provided a history at that 
point of picking up a computer when he fell and landed directly onto his right shoulder. Petitioner was 
noted to have an office job. He was referred for an MRI of the right shoulder for a potential rotator cuff 
tear. There was no notation of Petitioner not being able to work at that point. (PX1 p. 1166-1170).   
Petitioner returned to his PCP Dr. Aiyash on August 10, 2023 for his Type 2 diabetes. There was 
nothing noted about Petitioner’s shoulder pain. (PX4, p. 1124). 
On August 20, 2023, Petitioner presented to Amita Health Aurora. Petitioner was a 58-year-old 
male with a history of diabetes, hypertension, esophageal varices, presenting for an evaluation of neck 
pain. Petitioner stated he was pulling out of a parking spot when someone backed into the passenger side 
of his vehicle. Petitioner developed achiness on the sides of his neck, left greater than right. Petitioner was 
26IWCC0136

5 
 
given medications and was to return to his PCP. Petitioner was noted to be the restrained driver. (PX4, 
p.709-725). The Arbitrator notes this contradicts Petitioner’s testimony that he was not driving. (T.50). 
Petitioner later testified he was sitting in his car at the service department and one of the porters backed 
into the back of his car in the rear. (T.69). Both accounts differ than the medical note. 
Petitioner started therapy on September 18, 2023 at ATI. (PX3 p.45). Petitioner stated he fell in his 
house on his left shoulder and injured his right shoulder. He presented with decreased range of motion and 
signs of rotator cuff pain. There was no indication this was related to any work-related accident. Petitioner 
was to undergo therapy two times a week for six weeks. (PX3, p.45).  
On October 23, 2023, Petitioner presented to Castle Orthopedics with Dr. Sachin Bansal. Petitioner 
noted he had been in physical therapy for about four weeks for his right shoulder and neck. It was noted 
Petitioner was unemployed. Petitioner was diagnosed with cervicalgia, impingement of the right shoulder 
and degenerative disc disease of the cervical spine. Petitioner was to continue with therapy and return. If 
his pain persisted, he would proceed with an MRI of the cervical spine and shoulder. There was no mention 
of work restrictions. (PX1, p.1102-1107). The Arbitrator further notes there is no mention of any work 
accident.  
On October 27, 2023 Petitioner was discharged from therapy at ATI. (PX3, p.13).  
 Petitioner had a physical therapy cervical initial evaluation on November 21, 2023.  Petitioner was 
a right-handed man with a diagnosis of cervicalgia, degenerative disc of the cervical spine and right 
shoulder impingement. The history noted Petitioner had an original injury when he fell onto his right 
shoulder when moving the computer. Petitioner was to undergo 12 visits of therapy. (PX1, p.1043-1046). 
 
Petitioner returned to Castle Orthopedics on December 11, 2023 for complaints of pain in his right 
shoulder and noted intermittent neck discomfort. Given the persistent pain despite physical therapy, Dr. 
Bansal recommended an MRI of his cervical spine and right shoulder. Petitioner was not provided any 
restrictions or taken off of work. (PX1 p. 1009-1015). 
 
Petitioner underwent an MRI of the right shoulder on January 20, 2024 which revealed a posterior 
superior labral tear, with mild to moderate tendinosis of the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and subscapularis 
tendons. (PX1 p.908). 
 
On January 23, 2024, Petitioner wrote a letter to Dr. Aiyash and requested a work restriction from 
the date of the injury to his right shoulder, November 9, 2022 to the present for worker’s compensation 
insurance. Petitioner noted he was referred to Dr. Saleem for surgery. (PX1, p.898; RX1). 
 
Petitioner presented to Dr. Aiyash on February 1, 2024. Petitioner needed a letter for work and need 
a causation opinion for his current condition. Dr. Aiyash noted Petitioner had previously been injured on 
November 9, 2022 and is on a 5-pound weight restriction by Dr. Bansal. (PX1, p.870). The Arbitrator 
notes Petitioner was not taken off work by Dr. Bansal. This also does not constitute a causal connection 
opinion.  
 
On February 5, 2024 Dr. Bansal placed Petitioner on 5-pound lifting restrictions. The restrictions 
were placed through February 9, 2024. (PX7).  
26IWCC0136

6 
 
On February 9, 2024, Petitioner presented to Dr. Arif Saleem. Petitioner presented for an evaluation 
of his right shoulder. He had been having one year of shoulder pain. Petitioner recalls lifting a box of 
computers and having his arm jerked away from him. Petitioner used to work as a worker’s compensation 
claim adjuster. Petitioner was given an intra-articular injection and was to follow up in six to eight weeks. 
No off-work note was provided. (PX1, p.833-839).  
 
Petitioner continued with physical therapy for his cervical and right shoulder conditions. (PX1, 
p.654-805). 
 
Petitioner was seen at Castle Orthopedics for a follow-up on March 22, 2024 with Dr. Saleem. 
Petitioner noted the injection helped temporarily and that he was making progress in therapy. The

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW 
The Arbitrator adopts the above Findings of Fact in support of the Conclusions of Law set forth 
below.   
 
Decisions of an arbitrator shall be based exclusively on the evidence in the record of the proceeding 
and material that has been officially noticed. 820 ILCS 305/1.1(e). Credibility is the quality of a witness 
which renders his evidence worthy of belief. The Arbitrator, whose province it is to evaluate witness 
credibility, evaluates the demeanor of the witness and any external inconsistencies with his/her testimony.  
Where a claimant’s testimony is inconsistent with his/her actual behavior and conduct, the Commission 
has held that an award cannot stand. McDonald v. Industrial Commission, 39 Ill. 2d 396 (1968); Swift v. 
Industrial Commission, 52 Ill. 2d 490 (1972).  
 
It is the function of the Commission to judge the credibility of the witnesses and to resolve conflicts 
in the medical evidence and assign weight to witness testimony. O’Dette v. Industrial Commission, 79 
Ill.2d 249, 253, 403 N.E.2d 221, 223 (1980); Hosteny v. Workers’ Compensation Commission, 397 Ill. 
26IWCC0136

9 
 
App. 3d 665, 674 (2009).  Internal inconsistencies in a claimant’s testimony, as well as conflicts between 
the claimant’s testimony and medical records, may be taken to indicate unreliability. Gilbert v. Martin & 
Bayley/Hucks, 08 ILWC 004187 (2010). 
 
In this case the Arbitrator finds Petitioner’s testimony does not comport with the medical evidence 
submitted into trial.  
 
With respect to Issue (C) whether an Accident occurred that arose out of and in the course of 
Petitioner’s Employment with Respondent and with respect to Issue (F) is Petitioner’s Present 
Condition of Ill-Being Causally related to the injury, the Arbitrator finds as follows:  
A decision by the Commission cannot be based upon speculation or conjecture. Deere and 
Company v Industrial Commission, 47 Ill.2d 144, 265 N.E. 2d 129 (1970).  A Petitioner seeking an award 
before the Commission must prove by a preponderance of credible evidence each element of the claim. 
Illinois Institute of Technology v. Industrial Commission, 68 Ill.2d 236, 369 N.E.2d 853 (1977). Where a 
Petitioner fails to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that there exists a causal connection between 
work and the alleged condition of ill-being, compensation is to be denied. Id. The facts of each case must 
be closely analyzed to be fair to the employee, the employer, and to the employer’s workers’ compensation 
carrier. Three “D” Discount Store v Industrial Commission, 198 Ill.App. 3d 43, 556 N.E.2d 261, 144 
Ill.Dec. 794 (4th Dist. 1989).   
The burden is on the Petitioner seeking an award to prove by a preponderance of credible evidence 
all the elements of his claim, including the requirement that the injury complained of arose out of and in 
the course of his or her employment. Martin vs. Industrial Commission, 91 Ill.2d 288, 63 Ill.Dec. 1, 437 
N.E.2d 650 (1982). The mere existence of testimony does not require its acceptance. Smith v Industrial 
Commission, 98 Ill.2d 20, 455 N.E.2d 86 (1983). To argue to the contrary would require that an award be 
entered or affirmed whenever a claimant testified to an injury no matter how much his testimony might 
be contradicted by the evidence, or how evident it might be that his story is a fabricated afterthought.  U.S. 
Steel v Industrial Commission, 8 Ill.2d 407, 134 N.E. 2d 307 (1956).   
The Illinois Supreme Court has held that a claimant’s testimony standing alone may be accepted 
for the purposes of determining whether an accident occurred.  However, that testimony must be proved 
credible. Caterpillar Tractor vs. Industrial Commission, 83 Ill.2d 213, 413 N.E.2d 740 (1980). In addition, 
a claimant’s testimony must be considered with all the facts and circumstances that might not justify an 
award. Neal vs. Industrial Commission, 141 Ill.App.3d 289, 490 N.E.2d 124 (1986). Uncorroborated 
testimony will support an award for benefits only if consideration of all facts and circumstances support 
the decision.  See generally, Gallentine v. Industrial Commission, 147 Ill.Dec 353, 559 N.E.2d 526, 201 
Ill.App.3d 880 (2nd Dist. 1990), see also Seiber v Industrial Commission, 82 Ill.2d 87, 411 N.E.2d 249 
(1980), Caterpillar v Industrial Commission, 73 Ill.2d 311, 383 N.E.2d 220 (1978). It is the function of 
the Commission to judge the credibility of the witnesses and to resolve conflicts in the medical evidence 
and assign weight to the witness’ testimony.  O’Dette v. Industrial Commission, 79 Ill.2d 249, 253, 403 
N.E.2d 221, 223 (1980); Hosteny v Workers' Compensation Commission, 397 Ill.App. 3d 665, 674 (2009).

 The Arbitrator questions Petitioner’s veracity in his testimony and throughout the medical records.

the Arbitrator also finds the timing of the alleged accident suspect. It was established Petitioner had

also requested FMLA which was denied, but when asked about the denial on cross-examination claimed 
he did not believe it had been denied but when he presented to the doctor on November 14, 2024, he

9, 2022, and in fact believed he was still employed by TriStar as of the trial date. (T. 46, 71).  Despite this

was classified as unemployed. (PX1 p.1102-1107, PX4 p.17, 686, 724). The Arbitrator also questions

alleged work injury until after he received bills and even then, despite being a claims specialist with over 
20 years’ experience, he did not follow the proper procedure to report an injury. (T.17-18, PX6).   
Based on the testimony and medical evidence presented, the Arbitrator finds there are numerous 
inconsistencies between Petitioner’s testimony and the medical evidence. The Arbitrator, however, notes 
that Petitioner’s initial medical record does document a trip and fall at home. Although there is no work 
accident noted in the initial medical records the Arbitrator could be persuaded to believe Petitioner 
sustained a compensable work injury based on the contemporaneous medical records. In addition, 
Petitioner did notify someone at his employment about an alleged work accident on November 17, 2022, 
only two weeks after the alleged injury. As such, when weighing the evidence even with the 
inconsistencies in testimony, the Arbitrator finds that Petitioner may have sustained a work injury at home

The Arbitrator notes, however, Petitioner’s current condition is not related to any alleged work 
injury. The Arbitrator finds Petitioner reached MMI as of November 10, 2022, the date of the ER visit 
based on the gap of treatment, no causation opinion and Petitioner’s inconsistent testimony as described

A decision by the Commission cannot be based upon speculation or conjecture. Deere and 
Company v Industrial Commission, 47 Ill.2d 144, 265 N.E. 2d 129 (1970).  A Petitioner seeking an award 
before the Commission must prove by a preponderance of credible evidence each element of the claim. 
Illinois Institute of Technology v. Industrial Commission, 68 Ill.2d 236, 369 N.E.2d 853 (1977). Where a 
Petitioner fails to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that there exists a causal connection between 
work and the alleged condition of ill-being, compensation is to be denied. Id. The facts of each case must

be closely analyzed to be fair to the employee, the employer, and to the employer’s workers’ compensation 
carrier.  Three “D” Discount Store v Industrial Commission, 198 Ill.App. 3d 43, 556 N.E.2d 261, 144 
Ill.Dec. 794 (4th Dist. 1989).   
When a preexisting condition is present, a claimant must show that “a work-related accidental 
injury aggravated or accelerated the preexisting [condition] such that the employee’s current condition of 
ill-being can be said to have been causally connected to the work-related injury and not simply the result 
of a normal degenerative process of the preexisting condition.”  St. Elizabeth’s Hospital v. Workers’ 
Compensation Commission, 864 N.E.2d 266, 272-273 (5th Dist. 2007).  Even when a preexisting condition 
exists, recovery may be had if a claimant’s employment is a causative factor in his or her current condition 
of ill-being.  Sisbro, Inc. v. Industrial Commission, 797 N.E.2d 665 (2003). Allowing a claimant to recover 
under such circumstances is a corollary of the principle that employment need not be the sole or primary 
cause of a claimant’s condition.  Land & Lakes Co. v. Industrial Commission, 834 N.E.2d 583 (2d Dist. 
2005). 
It is axiomatic that the weight accorded an expert opinion is measured by the facts supporting it 
and the reasons given for it; an expert opinion cannot be based on guess, surmise, or conjecture. Wilfert v. 
Retirement Board, 318 Ill.App.3d 507, 514-15 (1st Dist. 2000).   
The Arbitrator notes it is Petitioner’s burden of proof to establish a causal connection to 
Petitioner’s current condition to the original injury. Petitioner sought treatment on November 10, 2022. 
Petitioner then saw his primary care physician in December of 2022, January 2023, and March of 2023 
without requesting treatment for his alleged injury. Petitioner does not seek treatment again until June 8, 
2023, when he underwent an X-ray, some 7 months later. There are no notes with this treatment, and it is 
not clear why Petitioner underwent X-rays. The Arbitrator notes Petitioner sought treatment with an 
orthopedic on July 13, 2023 but then again did not seek treatment consistently until after his August 2023 
motor vehicle accident. Petitioner then began treating for his right shoulder and neck. The Arbitrator finds 
Petitioner injured his neck in this alleged motor vehicle accident. The Arbitrator finds that the gap in 
treatment does not support an acute injury necessitating medical attention in regards to his right shoulder 
claim.   
In addition, the Arbitrator finds no treating physician opined Petitioner’s current condition is 
related to any work injury. No physician ever clarified what was related and what was not.  In fact, 
Petitioner requested a causal connection opinion several times and was directed to speak with orthopedics. 
No treating orthopedic physician opined Petitioner’s surgery or shoulder condition was related to the work 
injury. In fact, the medical records are silent in regards to the same. 
The Arbitrator finds Drs. Aiyash and Saleem did not provide any type of causation opinion or 
testimony relating Petitioner’s right shoulder condition to the original accident. Neither doctor provided 
an explanation in regards to the delay of onset of symptoms or why the shoulder condition would be 
related. Dr. Saleem prescribed surgery but does not provide any explanation or reasoning whether the 
chronic condition is related to the original injury.  The Arbitrator cannot speculate in regards to the same.

In contrast, Respondent provided the opinion of Dr. Neault who opined Petitioner sustained a 
temporary condition with the alleged work-related injury. He noted his right shoulder surgery addressed 
chronic, degenerative issues and not addressed any acute injury. He also noted his diabetes was likely why

Based on the medical reporting, the significant gap in medical care, the lack of causation of opinion 
from Petitioner’s treating physician and Dr. Neault’s opinion, the Arbitrator finds Petitioner has failed to 
meet his burden in establishing his condition of ill-being in regards to his right shoulder is causally related 
to the work incident of November 9, 2022.
